idiom_name: NewX constructor functions + consumer-owned interfaces + main as composition root
implementation_notes: Dependencies are ordinary function parameters: NewOrderService(db DB, logger *slog.Logger, clock Clock) stores them in the struct, and the interfaces it declares live in the consuming package (accept interfaces, return concrete types). What replaces the injector is main, or a small setup helper it calls: the call order is the dependency graph and the compiler checks every edge. wire and dig/fx exist for large graphs - and add indirection to something the language already does explicitly - so the hand-wired form stays the default.
pitfalls: Interfaces defined next to the implementation instead of the consumer invert the dependency arrow back - keep the seam in the using package.
Accepting a heavyweight concrete type (a global logger, a whole *sql.DB) in a constructor rebuilds hidden coupling; accept the narrow interface the package truly needs.
Wire/dig hide the graph: once the compiler stops showing the wiring, missing providers surface at generate time or at run time instead.

variants.name: google/wire compile-time code generation
variants.idiom_name: wire.NewSet provider sets + wire.Build injector generating wire_gen.go
variants.implementation_notes: wire moves the composition root into generated code: providers are plain constructors collected into wire.NewSet, an injector stub calls wire.Build(...), and the generated wire_gen.go contains explicit calls in dependency order. Unlike dig/fx it needs no reflection at run time and fails at generation time when a provider is missing, so the binary ships hand-written-quality wiring with compile-time graph checking. Use it where several binaries or test injectors make hand maintenance of the same wiring expensive.
pitfalls: Forgetting go generate ./... leaves the generated wiring stale after a constructor signature changes.
Provider sets are API: injecting bare types such as string or int without distinct wrapper types makes bindings collide.

variants.name: uber-go/dig and fx runtime container
variants.idiom_name: dig Provide + Invoke (fx adds modules and lifecycle hooks)
variants.implementation_notes: dig registers each constructor with Provide, inspects parameter and result types by reflection, and resolves the graph when Invoke asks for a type; fx adds modules plus OnStart/OnStop lifecycle ordering. The consumers stay constructor-injected - only the wiring is resolved at run time - which suits large service binaries that want one registration point and managed start-up/shutdown. The costs are reflection, weaker compile-time visibility and the service-locator temptation the dig README itself warns about.
pitfalls: Missing providers compile fine and fail at Invoke - keep a start-up test that builds the container.
Exposing the container to library code turns it into a service locator; resolve once at the edge and pass concrete dependencies.
